solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Film companion in company with backing singers

indicators.note: to back is to go backwards, so the word is read in reverse

blocks.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company
RATS are informers, who 'sing' to the police; turned round they give STAR

explanation.surface: A film crew's backing singers keep a star company on set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singers' looks musical, but in crossword slang a singer is an informer, a rat. 'In company with' is doing double duty: it supplies CO and joins it to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-star is an actor who shares the billing in a film, a companion on screen.

clue.text: Verify angry statement indicating threat to King

blocks.note: in chess, 'check' is announced when the king is under attack

explanation.surface: Someone checks an angry remark that sounds like a threat against the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The King is a chess king, not a monarch, and the statement is the single word a player says when attacking it.
explanation.definitionFit: To crosscheck something is to verify it against another source.

clue.text: Elves always labouring primarily to support Saint Nick

indicators.note: primarily = at first, so take the opening letter of each word
in a down clue the supporting piece sits below

blocks.note: ST is the usual abbreviation for saint
the first letters of Elves, Always, Labouring

explanation.surface: Santa's elves toil endlessly to back up Saint Nicholas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Nick' reads as Santa Claus; the phrase splits, with Saint in the wordplay and Nick, a British word for steal, as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick something is British slang for to steal it.

clue.text: Performer playing sitar with T. Rex regularly

indicators.note: playing = performing with, loosely arranging the letters
regularly = at regular intervals, taking every other letter

explanation.surface: A musician plays sitar alongside the glam-rock band T. Rex.
explanation.walkthrough: T. Rex was a 1970s British glam-rock band, which makes the sitar sound like a real session; here the name is only four letters to be thinned out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the French-flavoured word is used for singers, dancers and variety acts.

clue.text: Careless US cops stuck in window frame

indicators.note: one thing stuck in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a sash is the frame of a sash window

explanation.surface: Sloppy American police get stuck climbing through a window.
explanation.walkthrough: A sash window slides up and down in a frame, the sash; LAPD goes inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash work is done hastily and carelessly.

clue.text: Northern painter unhappy on railway

blocks.note: RY is the standard abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A gloomy northern artist sits on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: L. S. Lowry painted industrial Lancashire, famous for its matchstick figures; in a down clue 'on' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: L. S. Lowry was an English painter of northern mill towns.

clue.text: Bone in head completely inverted

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a down clue reads the letters backwards

blocks.note: pate = the top of the head

explanation.surface: A bone lodged in someone's head has been flipped right over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bone in head' pulls you towards the skull; the bone is the kneecap and 'in' only joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the kneecap's anatomical name, one particular bone.

clue.text: Key on piano sharp, it’s decided

blocks.note: p = piano, the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A musician settles on which key to play in on the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: Key, piano and sharp all look like music; only the first two are, and 'sharp' means pointed. In a down clue A sits 'on' P, above it.
explanation.definitionFit: An appointed time or place is one that has been decided in advance.

clue.text: Smog yellowish-brown mostly

indicators.note: most but not all of the word, so drop the last letter

blocks.note: HAZEL, a yellowish-brown colour, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A description of dirty, mostly brownish-yellow city air.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one weather report, so 'mostly' looks like it qualifies the colour rather than trimming a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A haze is a thin murk in the air, like smog.

clue.text: Mythical giant largely competent? That’s up for debate

indicators.note: largely = not quite entirely, so drop the last letter

blocks.note: ARGUS, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth, without his last letter

explanation.surface: Someone questions whether a legendary giant was really up to the job.
explanation.walkthrough: Argus Panoptes was the many-eyed giant set to guard Io; the clue reads as a sceptic's remark, with the question mark leading into the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something arguable is open to dispute, up for debate.

clue.text: Forcibly remove cricketer’s mistake

blocks.note: what rebels do to a ruler or a government
a fielder's throw that runs past the stumps and gives away extra runs

explanation.surface: A cricketer's blunder gets him forcibly thrown out of the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket, the English bat-and-ball game, gives the second sense: a wild return from the field that runs away and costs the team runs.
explanation.definitionFit: To overthrow is to remove from power by force; an overthrow is also that fielding error.

clue.text: Gemstone heading for Bolivian capital, skipping US city

indicators.note: skipping = leaving out, so the named letters are removed

blocks.note: LA PAZ, the seat of Bolivia's government, without LA, Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A gem smuggler bound for La Paz avoids stopping in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading' tempts you to take the first letter of Bolivian; here it means travelling towards, TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Topaz is a precious gemstone, usually yellow.

clue.text: Bully Parisians working out where Stonehenge is

indicators.note: working something out means reworking it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Intimidated Parisians try to find where Stonehenge is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' reads as solving a puzzle about the monument, which is exactly why it hides its job of rearranging letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain, a chalk plateau in Wiltshire, England.

clue.text: Train follower to offer entertaining trips north of Massachusetts?

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to hold them inside
in a down clue, north of means placed above

blocks.note: MA is the postal code for Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A tour company offers train excursions heading up past Massachusetts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' suggests the railway, but it is the long trail of a wedding dress, and the bridesmaid walks behind it. Massachusetts is a US state, and 'north of' puts it below the trips.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridesmaid follows the bride up the aisle, behind her train.

clue.text: Dispatch includes empty tube

indicators.note: with its contents taken out, leaving only the outside letters

explanation.surface: A parcel arrives containing nothing but an empty tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatch' looks like a parcel or a message; here it means speed, as in 'with all dispatch'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispatch can mean speed or promptness, which is haste.

clue.text: Web user is map nerd unfortunately

indicators.note: things gone badly wrong, so the letters are in the wrong order

explanation.surface: An internet user turns out to be a cartography geek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web user' reads as someone online; the web is a spider's, and the user is the comic-book hero who swings on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spider-Man shoots and swings on webs, a user of webs.

clue.text: Defame footballer briefly with glib speech

indicators.note: cut short, so drop the last letter

blocks.note: George BEST, the Manchester United footballer, cut short

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking pundit slanders a footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a famous Northern Irish footballer of the 1960s and a crossword favourite for BEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To bespatter someone is figuratively to splash mud on their name, to defame them.

clue.text: Stomped on sea creature biting lady

indicators.note: something biting another has it in its mouth

blocks.note: a squid is a sea creature
she = a lady, the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A squid bites a woman, who stamps on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomped on' is a past-tense verb, and the answer must match it; 'lady' for SHE is a common crossword swap of a person for their pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something squished has been crushed flat, stomped on.

clue.text: Liqueur with crushed ice ran out

indicators.note: crushed = broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drink served over crushed ice until the ice ran out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crushed ice' reads as a drinks order, so it is easy to stop the fodder at ICE; the whole of 'ice ran out' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a French orange-flavoured brand, one example of a liqueur.

clue.text: Pond dweller bit European

explanation.surface: Something living in a pond took a bite out of a European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit' reads as the past tense of bite; it is the noun, a small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is a young frog that lives in ponds.

clue.text: Storage device contains poem written in secret language

indicators.note: one thing containing another holds it inside

blocks.note: a CD, compact disc, stores data

explanation.surface: A disc holds a poem that has been written in cipher.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long phrase at the end, not 'Storage device'; the answer is an adjective, like 'written'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a message put into cipher has been encoded, so it is in a secret language.

clue.text: Sweet area within Middle East mount

indicators.note: to be within something is to be enclosed by it, so A goes inside the mountain's name

blocks.note: Mount Carmel, a mountain in Israel
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A sweet shop tucked into a Middle Eastern mountain area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' can suggest a camel you ride, and CAMEL is so close to the answer that it misleads; the mount is Mount Carmel, with A inside after CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A caramel is a chewy sweet made from cooked sugar.

clue.text: Judges source local addresses somehow?

indicators.note: somehow = in some unknown way, so the letters come out in another order

explanation.surface: Magistrates look up where people live in the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judges' looks like people on the bench; it is the Book of Judges in the Bible, fragments of which survive among the scrolls.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dead Sea Scrolls include some of the oldest texts of biblical books such as Judges.

clue.text: Do well fitting 90 into climbing shelter

indicators.note: fitting one thing into another puts it inside
'into' names the receiving word, the one that is fitted around the 90
in a down clue, climbing reads the word from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Climbers do well to squeeze ninety of them into a mountain hut.
explanation.walkthrough: A lee is the side of something sheltered from the wind, a standard crossword shelter; '90' is a Roman numeral, not a count.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to excel is to stand out, to do well.

clue.text: Unknown table-top game from the south is silly

indicators.note: in a down clue, starting from the south means reading upwards

blocks.note: pool is played on a table

explanation.surface: A mysterious board game from southern parts is daft.
explanation.walkthrough: YPOOL read from the bottom up gives LOOPY.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: someone gone loopy has gone a bit mad, daft.

clue.text: Rutter featured in playlist again?

indicators.note: to be featured in something is to appear inside it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the singer Rutter has turned up on a playlist once more.
explanation.walkthrough: John Rutter is an English composer of choral music, which makes the playlist sound natural; a rutter is also an animal in the rut, the mating season.
explanation.definitionFit: Stags rut, fighting for mates in autumn, so a stag is a rutter.

clue.text: Agency worker ending in no time

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: a temp is a temporary worker from an agency

explanation.surface: A temp's contract finishes almost immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In no time' reads as one phrase meaning quickly; it splits, with 'no' in the wordplay and 'time' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, the tempo is the time, the speed of the beat.

clue.text: Drink loads inside bars at closing time?

blocks.note: a coda is the closing passage of a piece of music, its final bars

explanation.surface: Someone downs lots of drink in pubs at last orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The bars are musical bars, not pubs, and closing time is the end of a piece, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream soda is a sweet, vanilla-flavoured fizzy drink.

clue.text: Redhead left custody at last with caution

indicators.note: the last letter of the word

blocks.note: ginger is a British nickname for a red-haired person

explanation.surface: A red-haired prisoner is finally released on a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left custody' reads as walking out of jail; 'left' is just L and 'custody' gives only its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: moving gingerly means moving carefully, as if afraid of hurting something.

clue.text: Greatly amused by rock band on the radio

indicators.note: heard on the radio, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: Slade were a 1970s British glam-rock band

explanation.surface: A listener was delighted by a rock band on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Slade, a 1970s British glam-rock band best known for 'Merry Xmas Everybody', supplies the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To slay an audience is to make them laugh uproariously, so slayed means greatly amused.
